nature-nbs-348.title: Levels of ecological organization
nature-nbs-348.text: Ecology sees the living world as a ladder. It runs from organisms to populations, guilds, communities, ecosystems, biomes and the biosphere. The biosphere is the largest scale, the sum of ecosystems on the planet, and ecological relationships regulate energy, nutrient and climate fluxes up to that scale. Community ecology studies how interactions among species and their environment affect species abundance, distribution and diversity. Holism holds that life self-organizes into layers of emergent whole systems with non-reducible properties.

nature-nbs-349.title: Niche construction: organisms that remake their habitats
nature-nbs-349.text: Organisms do not only face environmental pressures; they also modify their habitats. The feedback between organism and environment can act from local scales, like a beaver pond, to global ones. It persists even after death.

nature-nbs-346.title: Forest site preparation before planting
nature-nbs-346.text: A cleared forest site needs work before trees go back in. Forest site preparation applies treatments to ready the site for seeding or planting and to ease regeneration. Prescribed or broadcast burning prepares clearcut sites by reducing slash, plant competition and humus. Mounds create raised planting spots and improve outplant performance where soil is cold or wet: they averaged 10 and 7 degrees C warmer at 0.5 and 10 cm depth than controls. In a British Columbia trial, trees on south, east and west-facing microsites grew larger than on north-facing ones. Choice of planting spot mattered more than orientation.

nature-nbs-343.title: Primary and secondary tillage
nature-nbs-343.text: Tilling comes in two passes. Primary tillage is deeper and more thorough, usually done after harvest. It aims for a reasonable depth of soft soil, buries residues, kills weeds and aerates, and it leaves a rough surface. Secondary tillage is shallower and prepares the seedbed. It incorporates fertilizer, makes a finer tilth, levels the surface and controls weeds.

nature-nbs-344.title: Tillage classes by residue left on the surface
nature-nbs-344.text: One way to sort tillage is by what it leaves behind. Intensive tillage leaves under 15% residue cover on the soil surface. Reduced tillage leaves 15 to 30%, and conservation tillage at least 30% during the critical erosion period. That cover slows water movement and erosion. It also benefits predatory arthropods and saves fuel, labour and soil compaction.

nature-nbs-345.title: Zone tillage: working only the seed row
nature-nbs-345.text: Zone tillage is a modified deep tillage that tills only narrow strips and leaves the soil between rows untilled. The strip, about five inches wide, breaks plow pans, warms the soil and prepares a seedbed. This differs from {{ref:nature-nbs-290}}, which relies on residue that delays warming in northern climates.

nature-nbs-291.title: Conservation tillage: stirring the soil less
nature-nbs-291.text: Tilling has been used since at least 3000 B.C., and farmers have since found ways to do less of it. Conservation tillage is a group of practices that reduce how much the soil is tilled. It leaves at least 30% crop residue on the surface, which slows water movement and cuts soil erosion. No-till and strip tillage are both forms of it, though no-till is not the same thing. By 2014 more than 75% of Canadian Prairie cropland had adopted it.

nature-nbs-351.title: Polyculture: many crops in one field
nature-nbs-351.text:
Most farm fields today hold one crop, but that was not always so. Polyculture grows more than one crop species together in the same place at the same time, in contrast to monoculture. It was traditionally the most prevalent form of agriculture. Pesticides, herbicides and fertilizers made monoculture dominant in developed countries from the 1950s. Around 15% to 20% of the world's agriculture is estimated to still rely on traditional polyculture.

It raises total yield, stability and resource efficiency, though each crop's own yield is lower, and crops mainly compete for room, light, water and nutrients. Diverse crops reduce pest and disease losses; the disease-diversity hypothesis holds that more plant diversity lowers disease severity. Polyculture can also cut pesticide and fertilizer release and freshwater eutrophication, and deep-rooted legumes improve soil structure and drainage.

There are drawbacks. Mechanized sowing and spraying become difficult, more manual labour is needed, and compatible combinations can be hard to find.

nature-nbs-354.title: Living mulch: a second crop under the first
nature-nbs-354.text: A living mulch is a second crop sown beneath a main crop to cover the soil and reduce erosion. The covering crop can also serve as green manure. Living mulches have been popular under orchard trees and perennial vegetables such as asparagus.

nature-nbs-355.title: Mixed cropping: all the seeds sown together
nature-nbs-355.text: Mixed cropping is a polyculture in which all the seeds are mixed and sown together. The result mimics natural plant diversity and is simple to handle. The costs are that crops can compete, and any pesticide or fertilizer goes on all of them.

nature-nbs-353.title: Rice polyculture: fish and ducks in the paddy
nature-nbs-353.text: A rice paddy can feed more than the rice. Rice polyculture raises fish, ducks or both with rice on the same paddy. Rice-fish systems in South-East Asia and China add a valuable fish crop and reduce eutrophication of neighbouring rivers. An Indonesian variant combines rice, fish, ducks and water fern. The ducks eat weeds, the fern fixes nitrogen, and duck and fish manure reduce fertilizer needs.

nature-nbs-352.title: The Three Sisters: maize, beans and squash
nature-nbs-352.text:
Some farmers planted three crops in one mound. The Three Sisters is the traditional Central and North American intercropping of maize, beans and squash. The mixture can be traced back some 3,000 years to Mesoamerican civilizations.

Each plant does a different job. Maize gives the bean a structure to climb. The bean supplies nitrogen to all the plants. Squash suppresses weeds. Together they show the logic of {{ref:nature-nbs-351}}: crops chosen so that each helps the others rather than only competing.

nature-nbs-318.title: Introduced species: life moved by human hands
nature-nbs-318.text: Nearly all the food Americans eat comes from species that did not originate there: non-native crops and livestock account for 98% of US food. An introduced species is one living outside its native range after being brought there by human action. It is also called alien, exotic or non-native. Introductions are intentional, for economic gain, recreation or fixing problems such as erosion, or accidental, as with rats on ships or marine organisms in ballast water. Those that establish and spread are naturalized. Only those that spread widely or quickly and harm the environment, health, resources or economy are invasive. Whether an exotic will become invasive is seldom understood at the start.

nature-nbs-317.title: Food sovereignty: who controls the food system
nature-nbs-317.text:
Having enough food and controlling how it is grown are different questions. Food security is about access to enough food. Food sovereignty is the idea that people should control their own food systems, including how food is produced, distributed and consumed. Via Campesina coined the term in 1996. The 2007 Declaration of Nyeleni, from delegates of 80+ countries, defines it as peoples' right to healthy, culturally appropriate, ecologically sound food. As of 2020 at least seven countries had written it into their constitutions and laws.

The idea is argued over. Advocates say the Green Revolution raised output without solving hunger because it ignored access to land and economic power. Critics say the movement rests on wrong assumptions about subsistence farming. A related right is seed sovereignty, to breed and exchange open-sourced seeds, argued for on biodiversity and climate resilience grounds as well as food justice.

nature-clim-282.title: Electricity generation: turning other energy into power
nature-clim-282.text:
Electricity is not freely available in nature. It must be produced by transforming other forms of energy, in power stations, before delivery or storage. Most is made by electromechanical generators driven by heat engines, flowing water or wind. Only photovoltaic solar and fuel cells make commercial-scale electricity without a generator; almost all other commercial power comes from a turbine.

World generation in 2024 was 30,850 TWh: coal 34%, gas 22%, hydro 14%, nuclear 9%, wind 8%, solar 7%, oil and other fossil 3%, biomass 2%. How clean the supply is depends on where you live. Fossil fuels supply about 10% of electricity in France, 70% in the US and 80% in China.

Each source has costs. Coal plants supply about a third of world electricity but cause the most early deaths per unit of energy, mainly from air pollution. Gas plants are more efficient than coal and emit less carbon dioxide, but gas extraction releases significant methane. Hydropower supplied 15% of world electricity in 2023 and, with a dam and reservoir, can change output within seconds or minutes. Grids carry varying loads, and the daily minimum is the base load, often supplied by plants that run continuously.

nature-clim-280.title: Distributed generation: small power sources near the user
nature-clim-280.text:
The power station down the road may be a rooftop. Distributed generation uses small, grid-connected devices that generate and store electricity close to the load they serve, called distributed energy resources. Conventional power stations are centralised and often send power over long distances. Distributed resources are modular, sited near the load and have capacities of 10 MW or less.

Central plants' economies of scale began to fail in the late 1960s. By the early 21st century they arguably could no longer deliver cheap, reliable power to remote customers through the grid. The distributed resources include cogeneration, solar photovoltaics, small wind, microhydro, waste-to-energy and storage such as batteries, flywheels and vehicle-to-grid. They typically have high capital cost per kilowatt. Local production avoids transmission losses, which are generally 8-15% of energy on long lines and transformers. Solar-plus-battery stand-alone systems have a low levelized cost, so some authors think they may enable mass grid defection.

There are problems. Integration raises technical issues of power quality, voltage stability, harmonics, reliability, protection and control, and IEEE 1547 sets the interconnection standard. A single vendor's vulnerable control system used at thousands of sites could let one attacker disable them all, reversing decentralisation's benefits.

nature-clim-283.title: Smart grids: two-way electricity and information
nature-clim-283.text:
The classic grid was a one-way street. Classic grids were centralized systems of transmission, distribution and demand-driven control. A smart grid upgrades this 20th-century design with two-way communications and distributed intelligent devices, so electricity and information can both flow in both directions.

Smart grids use techniques such as state estimation to detect faults and self-heal without technician intervention. That improves reliability and reduces vulnerability to disasters or attacks. They handle bidirectional flows from rooftop solar and electric-car batteries, which classic grids did not expect: local over-generation can raise safety issues. Their flexibility allows more variable renewables such as solar and wind, even without added storage.

Demand response lets generators and loads coordinate in real time to flatten spikes. It avoids reserve generators and lets users run low-priority devices when energy is cheapest. Suppliers and consumers exchange price and willingness-to-pay signals, so only critical loads pay peak prices. Concerns centre on smart meters and their remote control and variable pricing, on cyberattack vulnerability, and on the need for a business case before a utility invests.
